stages.script: Start with one question before you touch the tracheostomy: does this child still have a usable upper airway? A tracheostomy creates a new route into the trachea below the larynx, but it does not automatically mean the mouth and nose are useless. Some children can still breathe from above if the tracheostomy fails. Others cannot. That distinction changes everything in an emergency, because it determines whether bag-mask ventilation through the face can rescue the child or whether the stoma is the only route to the lungs.

Now think about a fresh tracheostomy. The skin opening and the tracheal opening are new. They have not yet formed a stable tract. If you remove the tube, those two openings may no longer sit neatly in line. That is why an unnecessary early tube change is risky: the replacement tube can slide into soft tissue instead of the trachea. Maturation sutures help hold the openings together, and stay sutures can help bring the trachea forward. But notice the wording: an early change is risky, not forbidden. If the tube is completely blocked and the child cannot breathe, restoring oxygenation takes priority.

Why do these tiny tubes block so easily? Normally the nose warms, humidifies and filters inspired air. A tracheostomy bypasses much of that conditioning. Add a small paediatric lumen, post-operative dehydration, oxygen, drying medication or thick secretions, and the effective diameter can fall quickly. Humidity matters because it keeps secretions mobile. Hydration matters because dry secretions become tenacious. Suction matters, but suction should stay within the tube length. Going beyond the tube can traumatise the tracheal wall, causing bleeding and granulation. And securing tapes matters because a moving child can dislodge an unsecured airway.

After a fresh tracheostomy, look for a small group of important problems: obstruction, displacement, surgical emphysema, pneumothorax and significant bleeding. Surgical emphysema means air has escaped from the airway into the surrounding soft tissue. You may see swelling of the neck, face or upper chest, feel crepitus, or simply notice that tapes which were comfortable are becoming tight. But do not make the opposite error and blame every deterioration on the tracheostomy. If the tube is visibly in place and a suction catheter passes, move on through breathing and circulation. The child may be unwell for another reason.

In an emergency, the questions are simple. Is the tracheostomy tube actually in the neck? Can you pass a suction catheter? And can you oxygenate the child? Call for help and give oxygen while you answer those questions. Do not blindly ventilate through a tube that may be displaced. If the catheter passes, the tube is likely patent enough to keep moving through the assessment. If it does not pass and the child cannot breathe, complete obstruction becomes much more likely. In that situation, leaving a blocked tube in place simply because the tract is fresh may be more dangerous than removing it.

Suppose the tube is out and will not go back in easily. The worst response is repeated forceful attempts. In a fresh tract that can create a false passage, and positive pressure through a false passage can inflate the neck rather than the lungs. If the child has a usable upper airway and bag-mask ventilation through the face is working, keep oxygenating that way while expert help arrives. If there is no usable upper airway, the rescue route is through the stoma using an appropriate interface. The principle is the same in both situations: oxygenation is the goal. Successful tracheostomy replacement is not the goal at any cost.

What exactly is surgical emphysema? Air has left the airway and entered soft tissue. After a new tracheostomy, that may happen because air leaks around the fresh tract, because the tube has displaced, because the trachea has been injured, or because ventilation is being delivered through a tube that is not fully inside the trachea. Positive pressure makes this important. If the tube is malpositioned, each breath can force more air into tissue. That is why rapidly increasing swelling and tightening tapes should make you reassess tube position and ventilation immediately.

You also need to know the tube that is in the child's neck. Paediatric tracheostomy tubes are not interchangeable pieces of plastic. Tube length, diameter, flexibility, cuff design and MRI compatibility all affect management. Some flexible wire-reinforced tubes are useful in difficult anatomy but are not suitable for MRI. Cuffed tubes may be chosen when a tighter seal is needed for ventilation or airway protection, and the method of inflation and deflation depends on the tube design. In an emergency, knowing the hardware is part of knowing the airway.

Now put it together. A child is forty-eight hours after tracheostomy. The neck is becoming swollen, the tapes suddenly feel tighter, saturations are falling, and the suction catheter only passes a short distance. Do not treat those as four separate observations. Build one mechanism. A fresh tract makes displacement and obstruction more dangerous. If the tube is no longer correctly positioned, airflow is impaired and air may leak into tissue. Positive pressure can worsen that leak, producing surgical emphysema and tightening the tapes. The response is driven by airway patency and oxygenation. That is the logic you should remember, rather than a memorised list of disconnected steps.
